text: A pinhole in a hydraulic hose can inject oil straight through your skin.
It carries oil at high pressure to the parts of the machine that move.
It's built in layers: an inner tube that holds the oil,
steel wire that holds the pressure,
and a cover that protects the wire.
Every cycle, it flexes, and every pressure spike stretches it.
Over time, heat and pressure pulses fatigue it.
Where it rubs, the cover wears through. Then the wire rusts, and snaps.
Tight bends and twists strain it even more.
Until the tube gives way: a weep, a spray, or a burst.
Warning signs: worn or cracked covers, exposed wire, bulges, and wet fittings.
So: inspect hoses on a schedule.
Never feel for a leak with your hand. Use cardboard.
Guard hoses where they rub, and avoid twists and tight bends.
And replace damaged hoses with the system depressurised and locked out.
